title: Consistency & Replication Models
summary: The moment you keep more than one copy of your data, the copies can disagree. Consistency models are the precise rules for how much disagreement you'll tolerate for how much speed.

blocks.markdown:
Replication keeps copies of your data on multiple machines; consistency models are the contract for what a reader is allowed to see.

- **Replication** buys durability, availability, and read speed — but the copies can fall out of sync.
- A **consistency model** says which values a read may legally return given the writes so far.
- **Stronger** = hides the copies, feels like one machine, costs coordination and latency.
- **Weaker** = copies lag, you tolerate stale reads, but it's fast and stays available.

blocks.subTitle: Pick the model for the data
blocks.markdown:
Match the model to what the data can tolerate.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| One agreed value now (balances, locks) | Linearizable |
| "I must see my own edit" | Read-your-writes |
| Stay up, tolerate slightly stale | Quorum or eventual |
| Merge without coordination (counters) | CRDTs |

blocks.subTitle: Replication topologies
blocks.markdown:
Two patterns make and keep the copies.

- **Leader–follower** — all writes hit one leader, which streams its change log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) to followers that replay it. Reads go to the leader (fresh) or followers (maybe stale).
- **Leaderless** (Dynamo, Cassandra) — no single leader; a client writes to several replicas and reads from several, using quorums to stay correct.
- **Multi-leader** accepts writes in many regions but makes conflicts common — reserved for offline-capable apps.

blocks.subTitle: Sync vs async replication
blocks.markdown:
The big knob is *when the leader tells the client "done."*

- **Synchronous** — wait for follower acks before acking the client. No data loss on leader failure, but writes are as slow as the slowest follower and a down follower stalls writes.
- **Asynchronous** — ack immediately, ship to followers in the background. Fast and resilient to slow followers, but a leader crash loses any not-yet-replicated writes.
- **Semi-sync** — wait for *one* follower, then ack. You lose a write only if the leader and that follower die together.

blocks.subTitle: The consistency spectrum
blocks.markdown:
Four classic models, strongest to weakest — each implies the weaker ones.

![Consistency spectrum from strong to eventual](assets/consistency-replication/consistency-spectrum.svg)

- **Linearizable** — acts like one copy and respects real time; a read sees any write that finished before it started.
- **Sequential** — everyone agrees on one order, but it may lag real time.
- **Causal** — cause is always seen before effect; concurrent ops may be seen in any order.
- **Eventual** — the only promise: if writes stop, copies converge.

assets.alt: Consistency spectrum from strong to eventual

blocks.subTitle: Session guarantees
blocks.markdown:
Most "feels broken" moments are killed cheaply by promising consistency just for one client's session.

- **Read-your-writes** — after you write, your own reads always reflect it. Stops "I posted a comment, refreshed, it's gone."
- **Monotonic reads** — once you read a value, later reads never go backwards in time.
- **Consistent prefix** — you never see an effect before its cause (no reply before its message).

Reach for these *before* full strong consistency — they fix the bulk of complaints.

blocks.subTitle: Quorum consistency
blocks.markdown:
Leaderless systems create truth by **overlap**. With N replicas, write to W and read from R.

![Quorum overlap with N=3, W=2, R=2](assets/consistency-replication/quorum-overlap.svg)

- If **R + W > N**, every read set and write set share a node — the read touches the latest acked write.
- N=3, W=2, R=2 is the balanced default: tolerates one node down for both.
- The reader still picks the newest copy by version/timestamp; **read repair** writes the fresh value back to stale replicas.
- Trap: quorums give *overlap*, not linearizability.

assets.alt: Quorum overlap with N=3, W=2, R=2

blocks.subTitle: Conflict resolution
blocks.markdown:
When two writes race with no causal order, the system must converge to one value.

- **Last-write-wins (LWW)** — keep the highest timestamp, drop the other. Dead simple, but silently loses a real write and trusts synced clocks.
- **Vector clocks** — track "what versions each replica has seen" to *detect* whether one descends from the other or they're concurrent; concurrent siblings go to the app to merge.
- **CRDTs** — data types whose merge is commutative and idempotent, so concurrent updates converge automatically with no coordination.

blocks.subTitle: Replication lag
blocks.markdown:
**Lag** is the delay between a write landing on the leader and showing up on a follower — usually milliseconds, but *not bounded*.

![Read-your-writes broken by replication lag](assets/consistency-replication/read-your-writes.svg)

- Under load, a long query, or a catching-up replica, lag spikes to seconds or minutes.
- The session anomalies are all *lag anomalies*: they break exactly when a read hits a follower that's behind.
- "We use read replicas to scale reads" is never the whole story — you must decide what a just-wrote user sees.

blocks.subTitle: The axes you trade on
blocks.markdown:
Every choice here is a genuine trade, not a bug to fix.

- **Consistency vs latency** — stronger guarantees add coordination round-trips, even with zero failures (PACELC's "else").
- **Consistency vs availability** — during a partition you serve stale data or refuse to serve; you can't have both (CAP).
- **Durability vs write latency** — sync never loses acked writes but waits; async is fast but can drop the last few.
- **Simplicity vs correctness** — LWW is trivial but lossy; vector clocks and CRDTs are correct but add metadata.

blocks.subTitle: Rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Match the model to the data, not the other way round.

- **Money, inventory, locks, unique IDs** → linearizable. Wrong answers corrupt the business.
- **"I don't see my own change"** → add read-your-writes first; you rarely need full strong.
- **Survive partitions, stay up** → causal or eventual, and design UX to tolerate staleness.
- **Commutative writes** (counters, sets) → CRDTs for availability *and* correctness.
- **Can't afford to lose writes** → never use LWW as your only conflict strategy.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The named systems are these ideas in production.

- **DynamoDB** — leaderless, quorums, vector clocks; reads default eventual, with strongly-consistent reads per call. **Tunable consistency**.
- **Cassandra** — per-query levels `ONE`/`QUORUM`/`ALL`; you write `R+W>N` into each statement. LWW by timestamp ([nosql-distributed-data](nosql-distributed-data)).
- **Spanner** — TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) plus commit-wait buys global linearizability across continents.
- **Postgres/MySQL** — leader–follower with async or sync/semi-sync standbys ([relational-db-internals](relational-db-internals)).

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Eventual means usually wrong."** No — it just promises no *upper bound* on convergence; the median is milliseconds, the danger is the tail.
- **"Read replicas just make reads faster."** They also make reads *stale* — you opted into lag anomalies.
- **"Quorum gives strong consistency."** It gives overlap, not a global order; concurrent writes still need consensus.
- **"LWW is a safe default."** It silently drops a concurrent write and trusts cross-machine clocks.
- **"Stronger is always better."** It also reduces availability — match the model to the data.
